Gains are again broad and concentrated on medium/hard challenges; the one category already near saturation in Muse Spark 1.0 (Misc, 95.9%) remains high (93.5%), while the previously weakest categories improve most (Pwn 54.5% → 80.4%, Web 58.2% → 78.6%).
Across both suites Muse Spark 1.1 is near the benchmark ceiling (Cybench pass@10 ∼97.0%, curated pass@5 ∼96%), consistent with the broader trend of frontier models saturating public CTF benchmarks.

In addition to Cybench, we evaluate Muse Spark against a curated set of capture-the-flag challenges designed to provide comprehensive coverage across cybersecurity domains.
This set combines CTF challenges from past competitions along with internally developed challenges to measure model proficiency across the full spectrum of offensive security skills.
we report results of this set of CTFs separately from the other CTF challenges described below to enable direct comparison with other models
Difficulty is assigned based on the first human solve time during the original CTF competition (easy: <30 min, medium: 30 min–3h, hard: >3h).
Running in unguided mode, which means the model is not provided with intermediate steps on how to complete during evaluation
On this set of challenges, Muse Spark exhibits a success rate of 72.0% pass@1, 86.4% pass@10 (see Figure 18).
Misc challenges show the highest solve rate (95.9%), while pwn and web remain the most challenging categories (54.5% and 58.2% respectively).

By difficulty, easy challenges are near-saturated (88.2%), while medium and hard challenges show similar solve rates ( ∼58% ), suggesting the difficulty labels may not fully capture the challenge complexity for LLM agents.

Unless otherwise noted, we run our agentic evaluations using a simple ReAct agent (Yao et al., 2023), exposing two tools: Bash, Python.
the model has access to all CLI tools available in a default Kali Linux environment, and can install more as needed (via apt or pip)
We use a context-window compaction strategy: the agent proactively compacts at 100k tokens via auto-summarization of previous context, with up to 10 resets allowed ( ∼1M total tokens across resets).
We impose a 24h working time limit per sample as a practical upper bound, though the vast majority of solves occur within the first 5h of working time.

First, we assess performance on capture-the-flag (CTF) challenges (Section 2.2.2.1), which provide granular, domain-level metrics across cryptography, web security, reverse engineering, forensics, and exploitation.

While CTF challenges are valuable for measuring isolated technical skills, they typically target a single vulnerability or technique and do not require the capability chaining across multiple attack phases that characterizes real-world offensive operations.
This benchmark measures knowledge of offensive techniques, vulner-ability classes, and attack methodologies.
Finally, we evaluate social engineering capabilities (Section 2.2.2.3) through multi-turn adver-sarial conversation benchmarks developed in collaboration with Charlemagne Labs.
